notes: “A hairy man” may describe Elijah himself or a hairy garment. The leather belt is explicit.
The fire consumes the captain and his fifty men. The narrative repeats the deaths of the second group; it does not explain away the harm.
The two kings named Jehoram belong to different kingdoms. This accession is dated to Judah’s Jehoram’s second year; 3:1 dates it by Jehoshaphat’s eighteenth year. Both notices are retained.
vocabulary: The name of the god consulted at Ekron; the story contrasts that consultation with seeking Israel’s God.
A title used for a prophet.

notes: A “double share” evokes the firstborn’s inheritance portion. It need not mean twice Elijah’s miraculous power.
The fiery chariot separates the men; the text says Elijah ascends in the whirlwind.
The Hebrew words rendered “he too” are difficult to place. They can be joined to Elisha’s action or to the preceding question.
The word describing the land can mean causing miscarriage, bereavement, or barrenness. The related wording in verse 21 is kept broad as loss of life.

The Hebrew calls the mockers young boys and then children. It gives no basis for turning them into an armed adult gang. The bears tear forty-two of them; the text does not explicitly say all forty-two die.
vocabulary: Literally “sons of the prophets”: a prophetic group, not necessarily biological sons.
Elijah’s outer garment, carried into Elisha’s ministry.
The taunt uses an ascent verb also prominent in Elijah’s departure.

notes: The Hebrew can be heard as an instruction to make ditches or as a declaration that the valley will become full of pools.
The destruction of trees, springs, and farmland is explicit both in the prediction and in its execution in verse 25.
The king offers his firstborn son as a burnt offering. The “great wrath” against Israel is not assigned an explicit source: divine wrath and human fury are among the interpretations.
vocabulary: Goods paid by a subordinate ruler to an overlord.
The instrument player accompanies the prophetic scene; the text does not describe the music.
An offering consumed by fire on the altar.

notes: The creditor threatens to take the woman’s two children as slaves. This is debt enslavement, not ordinary hired work.
“This time next year” renders a Hebrew expression also used in the promise to Sarah; its literal wording refers to the season of life.
The woman’s reply uses shalom, “peace” or “well-being.” The repeated reply in verse 26 does not disclose her son’s death.
Gehazi’s staff does not wake the boy. That failed attempt remains distinct from Elisha’s later actions.
The boy sneezes seven times. The number and the bodily actions are retained without diagnosing a medical procedure.
vocabulary: The beginning of a lunar month, associated with communal worship.
The first produce brought as an offering.

notes: The LORD is credited with giving victory to Aram, Israel’s enemy. The skin condition is tzaraat, a broad ancient category, not a secure diagnosis of modern leprosy.
The young girl was captured in a raid and serves Naaman’s wife. The narrative gives no account of her consent or emotional state.
The read tradition names Amana; the written text has Abana.
Naaman asks for two mule loads of earth and declares exclusive sacrifice to the LORD. The text does not explicitly explain the earth’s intended use.
Naaman anticipates bowing while supporting his master in Rimmon’s temple. Elisha’s “Go in peace” is retained without expanding it into a general rule about worship.
vocabulary: Ancient units of weight, used here for silver and gold.
Part of Elisha’s list of possessions and dependents in his rebuke of Gehazi.

notes: The axhead was borrowed. Its loss is therefore also an obligation to another person.
The unusual word for blindness may describe a disabling confusion of sight. The account does not explain its physical mechanism.

“Dove dung” follows the Hebrew’s written and read expressions. Some understand the phrase as a name for a food plant. The price is five silver pieces for a quarter-kab, against eighty for a donkey’s head.
The opening can be read conditionally, “If the LORD does not help you,” or as a negative wish, “May the LORD not help you.” The Hebrew is terse.
The messenger arrives, but the final speaker is not explicitly identified. The words may be the king’s, whether spoken by him or relayed by his messenger.
vocabulary: A royal name used by more than one Aramean king.
A small dry measure; the text gives a quarter of it.
Coarse cloth worn as a sign of grief or distress.

notes: The soldiers imagine several Hittite kings and several kings of Egypt. This is their explanation of the sound, not the narrator’s report of actual reinforcements.
The repeated comparison with Israelites who remain and those who have perished is compressed and difficult. It places the proposed scouts under the same desperate conditions.
The repeated prophecy and response in verses 18–20 make the connection between seeing the food and not eating it explicit.
vocabulary: A dry measure used for grain and flour.
A unit of weight used to measure silver.
News of the abandoned camp and available food, which the men recognize must be shared.

notes: The read text is “tell him”; the written text has “not,” allowing “You will certainly not recover.” The draft follows the read tradition and retains the ensuing declaration that the king will die.
The Hebrew does not clearly identify whose fixed gaze causes whose discomfort.
The predicted harm includes killing children and ripping open pregnant women. Hazael’s “great thing” in verse 13 is not rewritten as a denial of moral capacity.
Jehoram and Joram are forms of the same name, borne here by kings of Judah and Israel. The overlapping reign notice is retained.
Ahaziah is twenty-two here. Athaliah is called Omri’s daughter; “daughter” can also refer to a later female descendant.
vocabulary: Hebrew saris can denote a court officer or a eunuch; the role is clear here, the bodily status is not.
An image for the continuation of David’s royal line.

notes: The Hebrew uses a coarse expression for males, literally those who urinate against a wall. The paired terms rendered “bound or free” are uncertain social categories.
The precise meaning of the expression for the bare or upper steps is uncertain.
“Whoring” is an accusation associated with religious infidelity. This speech does not establish a separate sexual biography of Jezebel.
This recalled oracle mentions Naboth’s sons as well as Naboth. The earlier account in 1 Kings 21 does not narrate their deaths.
This verse gives the eleventh year of Joram; 8:25 gives the twelfth. Both source notices are preserved.
Zimri also killed his royal master and briefly took the throne; Jezebel’s address recalls that earlier coup.
vocabulary: Pour oil on someone as a sign of appointment.
Male court attendants; the Hebrew title can also be used more broadly for officials.

notes: The Hebrew addresses Jezreel’s leaders while locating the recipients in Samaria. The place name is retained rather than emended.
The declaration “You are innocent” belongs to Jehu’s public defense, not to the narrator’s verdict.
The Hebrew “brothers” can refer to a wider kin group; the draft uses “relatives.”
The final expression is literally something like “the city of the house of Baal.” Its architectural meaning is uncertain; “inner part” is a contextual rendering.
The approval concerns action against Ahab’s house. Verses 29 and 31 explicitly qualify Jehu’s overall conduct.
vocabulary: The center of intention and loyalty, used here in a pledge of alliance.
The cult site is deliberately degraded for ordinary waste use.
Hebrew torah: teaching or law that is to guide conduct.

notes: The final Hebrew word in the guard order is uncertain. “Keep a close watch” conveys the context without supplying a detailed arrangement the wording cannot securely establish.
“Testimony” may refer to a covenant document or royal obligations. Its exact physical form is not specified.
The killing takes place at the palace, following the explicit order not to kill Athaliah in the LORD’s house.
Public 11:21 corresponds to Hebrew 12:1; the public verses of chapter 12 are one lower than their Hebrew labels.
vocabulary: A named group of royal guards.
Pour oil on the new king as part of his installation.
A binding relationship with stated obligations; two relationships are named here.

notes: The Hebrew connects Joash’s right conduct with Jehoiada’s instruction. It can be read as conduct during his instruction or throughout his days because of that instruction.
The first money category is difficult: it may refer to census payments or money that passes as currency. The other categories concern personal assessments and voluntary gifts.
The account says the paymasters acted faithfully. It does not accuse the earlier collectors of theft.
The pinned Hebrew names Jozabad and Jehozabad here. Other textual forms and the parallel in Chronicles differ; the names have not been silently harmonized.
vocabulary: Money set apart for the sanctuary.
Distinct offerings whose payments here belong to the priests.
A store of valuables, not a modern bank account.

notes: The deliverer is not named in this verse.
Joash and Jehoash are forms of the same name. The text distinguishes the kings of Israel and Judah by their fathers and kingdoms.
The instruction to strike the ground does not state whether the arrows are shot into it or struck against it by hand.
The dead man revives on contact with Elisha’s bones. The narrative gives no extended explanation or instruction about later practices.
vocabulary: The cry recalls Elisha’s words at Elijah’s departure in 2:12.
The promise relationship with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob remains a reason for compassion.

notes: Jehoaddan follows the source’s read tradition; its written form is Jehoaddin.
The quoted rule also appears in Deuteronomy 24:16. It distinguishes a killer’s guilt from that of his children.
The thistle-and-cedar fable mocks Amaziah’s claim to equal standing. The draft preserves the images and leaves their application in the king’s own warning.
The Hebrew connection between Damascus, Hamath, Judah, and Israel is difficult. “Which had belonged to Judah” is one way of construing it; the precise political relationship is uncertain.
vocabulary: An ancient length based on the forearm.
An image of erasing a people’s continued existence and remembrance.

notes: The separate house is described by an unusual term associated with freedom or separation. Kings does not give the explanation for the skin disease found in Chronicles.
Uzziah and Azariah name the same Judean king in this account.
Tiphsah is the Hebrew place name here. Its location in this episode is difficult; the draft does not replace it with another town. The attack on pregnant women is explicit.
Argob and Arieh are retained as named persons. Their exact role in the coup is not explained.
The twentieth year of Jotham is retained alongside the sixteen-year reign in verse 33; the draft does not impose a chronological reconstruction.
vocabulary: A large unit of weight; a thousand talents represents a substantial payment.
A smaller weight used to measure the silver levy.
Forcibly remove a population to another territory.

notes: Passing a child through fire occurs in the context of prohibited sacrificial practices. The wording is retained without treating it as a harmless ceremony.
The written text has Arameans, while the read tradition has Edomites. The earlier phrase still says Elath was recovered for Aram.
“For me to inquire by” is one reading of the bronze altar’s purpose. The verb may also mean examining or considering what to do with it.
The precise layout of the Sabbath passage and royal entrance, and the exact alteration, are uncertain. The stated connection to Assyria is retained.
vocabulary: Language of submission to a powerful ruler, not a literal adoption statement.
A sacrifice associated with peace, thanksgiving, or shared fellowship.
The large bronze basin made for the temple.

notes: “They followed what was empty and became empty” preserves a repeated Hebrew root. The object of misplaced worship shapes the description of the worshipers.
Both sons and daughters are named in the fire rites.
The account concerns peoples forcibly relocated into Samaria. It should not be turned into a claim about the character of all later Samaritans.
Verses 33 and 41 say the settlers feared the LORD while serving other gods; verse 34 says they did not fear the LORD. The shifts in description and evaluation are left visible.
vocabulary: Cult objects associated with Asherah worship.
A designation for a person who receives prophetic insight.
In these worship statements, reverence and religious allegiance, not only an emotion.

notes: Nehushtan resembles the Hebrew words for bronze and serpent. The naming clause can mean “he called it” or “it was called.”
The exceptional praise concerns Hezekiah’s trust. Josiah receives similarly exceptional praise for turning to the LORD in 23:25.
The envoy treats the removal of local altars as a reason to distrust the LORD’s help. That argument is part of his speech, not the narrator’s explanation.
The claim that the LORD ordered the invasion is the Assyrian speaker’s claim.
The written expressions are coarse; the read tradition substitutes more decorous terms. Both describe eating excrement and drinking urine under siege.
vocabulary: Assyrian official titles, conventionally understood as commander, chief court officer, and chief cupbearer or senior envoy.
Aramaic was understood by the officials; Judean was the local language understood by the listeners on the wall.
Familiar images of settled agricultural well-being used in the surrender offer.

notes: The promised “spirit” may be understood as an impulse or disposition, or as a spirit acting on the king. The text does not specify further.
Zion and Jerusalem are personified as daughters. “Virgin” is retained as part of the poetic address, not converted into a claim about individual residents.
“Of Armies” is supplied in the source’s read tradition though absent from its written consonantal line.
The stated number is 185,000. No plague, disease, or other natural mechanism is named.
“His sons” is present as a read addition in the pinned source. The account does not specify the interval between the withdrawal and the assassination.
vocabulary: Heavenly beings associated with the divine throne; the temple also contained their representations.
A name associated with Jerusalem and its holy hill.
Images of forcibly leading the proud invader back.

notes: The read text says “courtyard”; the written text has “city.”
The Hebrew says steps or degrees. The text describes the shadow’s movement on Ahaz’s steps without explaining the instrument or mechanism.
The pinned Kings text has Berodach-baladan; Isaiah 39 has Merodach-baladan.
Kings says Hezekiah listened to the visitors. It is not replaced with Isaiah’s different wording about his reaction.
Saris can mean a eunuch or a court official. “Eunuchs” preserves the possible bodily consequence of forced royal service.
Hezekiah’s response is retained without labeling it either selfish relief or exemplary acceptance.
vocabulary: Give instructions for the affairs of the household before death.
The dynastic promise remains a recurring reason for the city’s defense.
A store of valuables, including precious materials and equipment.

notes: The son’s fire rite belongs with the account’s prohibited practices; the text does not explain the mechanics.
The measuring line and plumb line connect Jerusalem’s judgment to Samaria and Ahab’s house. The wiped and overturned dish is a separate image of emptying.
Innocent bloodshed is expressly added to the cultic sins. The victims are not individually identified.
Kings’ account does not include the later repentance narrative found in Chronicles; it is not inserted here.
vocabulary: The heavenly bodies or host treated here as objects of worship.
The people belonging to the LORD, described as his allotted possession.

notes: The text calls the discovery the Book of the Instruction, using torah. Its exact extent is not stated.
Huldah is explicitly a female prophet. Her oracle is delivered directly to the royal delegation.

The promise of burial “in peace” stands beside Josiah’s later violent death in 23:29–30. The oracle also says he will not see the coming disaster on this place. The draft leaves both statements intact.
vocabulary: Hebrew torah: authoritative teaching or law.
A receptive response to the warning, shown here in humility and mourning.

notes: The male shrine attendants are traditionally called male cult prostitutes; their precise role is debated. The woven “houses” for Asherah may be textile coverings or shrine hangings.
The displaced priests share unleavened bread but do not serve at Jerusalem’s altar; the two statements are distinct.
Josiah kills the high-place priests on their altars. The Hebrew uses a verb also used for slaughtering sacrifices.
“No Passover like this” does not necessarily mean that no Passover of any kind had occurred during the intervening period.

The preposition connecting Neco’s march to Assyria can be understood as “to” or “against.” The draft leaves the military alliance unstated. Kings says Josiah was killed at Megiddo and carried away dead.
vocabulary: The discovered book described in terms of the binding relationship it sets out.
A place in the Valley of Ben-hinnom associated here with child sacrifice.
The Hebrew designation for the hill associated with these shrines.

notes: Jehoiachin is eighteen here, with a three-month reign. The age and duration have not been changed to match Chronicles.

The broad “all Jerusalem” is qualified by the poorest people remaining. Verses 14 and 16 give a total and selected subgroups; the draft preserves the figures without manufacturing an additional total.
Mattaniah is Jehoiachin’s uncle, and Babylon’s king renames him Zedekiah. He is not Jehoiachin’s son in this account.
vocabulary: The group associated with Babylon’s ruling power and armies in these accounts.
A boundary watercourse distinct from the Nile.
A subordinate king remains on a throne under an imperial ruler’s control; here that control also includes imprisonment and replacement.

sections.22: Gedaliah and the flight to Egypt

notes: Kings gives the ninth day but omits the month in this verse. The fourth month given in Jeremiah 52 is not silently added.
Zedekiah witnesses his sons’ deaths before his own eyes are put out. The sequence is explicit.
The arrival is dated to the seventh day here, compared with the tenth in Jeremiah 52:12.
The capitals are three cubits high in this verse. Other temple descriptions give five; this local figure is retained.
Kings names five royal advisers; Jeremiah 52 names seven. The counts are not harmonized.
“Lifted his head” recalls a release-and-favor idiom. The book ends with provision for the exiled king, not a narrated restoration of Judah’s kingdom.
vocabulary: Structures built to surround and attack a fortified city.
The name of the Babylonian ruler who releases Jehoiachin; “Evil” here is part of the traditional name, not an English moral description.
